content: In September 2013, a final consensus meeting was held in Geneva, attended by all members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG). During this meeting, a comprehensive review of evidence, assessments, and evaluations was conducted to refine and approve the final recommendations. The materials for this process were prepared under the supervision of the Department of HIV/AIDS. The meeting's objectives included reviewing evidence summaries, risk-benefit analyses, feasibility, costs, and acceptability of proposed recommendations. Additionally, the group reviewed draft recommendations, developed consensus on their strength, identified implementation steps and tools, and proposed future research priorities. Decisions were made by consensus, ensuring agreement on the wording of recommendations without significant dissent. Comments from the GDG and Steering Group were documented, summarized, and incorporated into the final recommendations. Any opposing views were resolved through discussion. Based on the quality of evidence and risk/benefit analyses, the guideline panel determined whether to issue strong, conditional, or no recommendations. In cases where consensus could not be reached, decisions were made by voting. After the meeting, draft guidelines were circulated to the GDG and Peer Review Group for feedback, which was incorporated as appropriate. An advisory group on Kaposi sarcoma (KS) also participated in teleconferences and provided input on drafts of that section. The GDG emphasized a public health approach, particularly considering resource availability in lowand middle-income settings. They identified critical knowledge gaps requiring primary research, especially for recommendations based on low or very low-quality evidence. Conversely, recommendations supported by moderate or high-quality evidence were not prioritized for further research. Identified research gaps were prioritized based on feasibility, innovation, equity promotion, and potential to improve management of the conditions addressed in the guidelines. The recommendations will be regularly updated as new evidence becomes available, with major reviews occurring at least every five years. The next major update is planned for 2019 under the oversight of the WHO Guidelines Review Committee (GRC). Simultaneously, a multi-agency group led by WHO developed a diagnostic tool for HIV/AIDS-related skin conditions. While the guidelines focus on treatment, this tool emphasizes diagnosis and complements the recommendations. The tool was developed through expert input from dermatologists specializing in HIV dermatology and underwent iterative refinement to improve diagnostic criteria and include additional relevant diagnoses and images. Field surveys were conducted in clinics across Africa to test the tool's utility, with practitioners using it to diagnose HIV-infected children and adults. The tool demonstrated 90% agreement between field practitioners and dermatologists in a pilot study. The next iteration of the tool will include globally relevant skin diseases and highlight conditions warranting HIV testing or biopsy. Plans are underway for broader production and further field testing. The guidelines also outline principles for HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and general care. All individuals with unknown HIV status presenting with conditions covered in the guidelines should be offered immediate HIV testing. Known HIV-positive individuals presenting with these conditions should be evaluated for ART eligibility. Early ART initiation is associated with clinical and prevention benefits, improving survival and reducing HIV incidence at the community level. Current WHO guidance recommends ART for all individuals with HIV and a CD4 count of 500 cells/mm³ or less, prioritizing those with advanced disease or a CD4 count of 350 cells/mm³ or less. ART is also recommended for individuals with active tuberculosis, hepatitis B with severe liver disease, pregnant and breastfeeding women, children under five, and those in serodiscordant relationships, regardless of CD4 count. The guidelines recommend simplified, less toxic, and more convenient ART regimens, ideally as once-daily fixed-dose combinations. For children under three years, such regimens may not yet be available. Referral to higher-level health facilities should be considered if conditions do not respond to recommended treatments. Kaposi sarcoma (KS), an AIDS-defining illness caused by human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), remains the most common malignancy in people living with HIV, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. KS lesions typically appear as macules, papules, nodules, or plaques, ranging in color from pink to purple to brown. They may also involve oral and genital mucosa, with or without internal organ involvement. Dissemination to lymphatics can occur, sometimes causing painful lymphedema or lymphadenopathy. In children, KS may present differently, often without characteristic skin lesions, which has implications for staging and treatment. Treatment strategies for KS have evolved with the advent of ART. Immediate ART initiation is recommended for all patients with KS, regardless of disease stage, to improve survival and reduce morbidity. For severe or symptomatic KS, systemic chemotherapy in combination with ART is recommended. Common chemotherapy regimens include vincristine with bleomycin and doxorubicin (ABV), bleomycin with vincristine (BV), and liposomal anthracyclines (doxorubicin or daunorubicin) when available. ART alone may suffice for less extensive skin involvement. Localized therapies, such as radiotherapy, topical therapy, and intralesional chemotherapy, may be used for symptomatic local disease or cosmetic purposes. The GDG emphasized the importance of prompt ART initiation as the most critical intervention for KS patients, improving survival and reducing opportunistic infections. While ART alone may induce KS lesion regression, chemotherapy can accelerate regression and remission of significant lesions, alleviate symptoms, and improve quality of life. However, chemotherapy carries potential toxicities and challenges, including limited access and high costs in resource-limited settings. Selection criteria for chemotherapy in addition to ART remain undefined, though T staging is often used to guide treatment planning.
